lessons.title: Power integration, definite integrals and improper endpoints
lessons.summary: Reverse the power and chain rules, evaluate with the correct limits and test an unbounded endpoint using a limit.
lessons.objective: Find complete power antiderivatives, evaluate signed definite integrals and recognise simple convergent or divergent improper integrals.
lessons.before: Recall rational indices, expanding brackets, derivatives of powers and the chain rule.
lessons.ideas:
Integration reverses differentiation

\[\int x^n\,dx=\frac{x^{n+1}}{n+1}+C,\qquad n\ne-1.\]

Increase the power before dividing. Rewrite roots and reciprocals with rational indices and integrate each term. Expand a product when that makes the powers easier to read. The constant is needed because differentiating it gives zero.

A linear inner expression brings a divisor

\[\int (ax+b)^n\,dx=\frac{(ax+b)^{n+1}}{a(n+1)}+C,\quad a\ne0,\ n\ne-1.\]

Differentiate the proposed answer to check both factors. If the original integrand has an excluded input, integration does not restore it. The power rule does not cover \(x^{-1}\); logarithmic integration belongs to a later course.

A definite integral is signed

\[\int_a^b f(x)\,dx=F(b)-F(a).\]

Use upper minus lower, including brackets around a negative lower value. An arbitrary constant cancels. Reversing the limits changes the sign; a negative answer can be a correct signed integral.

An undefined endpoint needs a one-sided limit

\[\int_0^b x^{-\frac12}\,dx=\lim_{\varepsilon\to0^+}\bigl[2\sqrt{x}\bigr]_{\varepsilon}^{b}.\]

Do not substitute into an undefined integrand. Test the antiderivative difference as the boundary is approached from inside the domain. A finite limit gives a convergent improper integral; an infinite limit is not a finite area. At an infinite endpoint, take the corresponding limit instead of treating infinity as an ordinary number.
lessons.method:
1. Rewrite the integrand and retain its domain.
  2. Integrate and check the result by differentiation.
  3. For an indefinite integral include a constant or use the supplied condition.
  4. For a definite integral use upper minus lower; use a limit at an improper endpoint.
mistakes: Increase the index before dividing.
Retain the reciprocal inner multiplier.
A definite integral is not automatically a geometric area.
An unbounded integrand can have a finite improper integral.

examples.title: Roots and reciprocal powers in one integral
examples.question: Find \(\int(6\sqrt{x}-4x^{-2}+3)\,dx\) on \(x>0\).
examples.solution:
\[\int(6x^{\frac12}-4x^{-2}+3)\,dx=4x^{\frac32}+\frac4x+3x+C.\]

Differentiating gives the original integrand. In particular, the derivative of \(\frac4x\) is negative. The original domain remains \(x>0\).

examples.title: Divide by both the new power and the inner gradient
examples.question: Find \(\int(3x-2)^4\,dx\).
examples.solution:
\[\int(3x-2)^4\,dx=\frac{(3x-2)^5}{15}+C.\]

The derivative multiplies by both 5 and 3; the denominator 15 reverses both factors.

examples.title: Keep the order of the limits
examples.question: Evaluate \(\int_1^{-1}(x^2-1)\,dx\).
examples.solution:
\[\left[\frac{x^3}{3}-x\right]_1^{-1}=\frac23-\left(-\frac23\right)=\frac43.\]

The integrand is non-positive between the endpoints, but the limits are reversed. With limits from \(-1\) to 1 the signed answer is \(-\frac43\).

examples.title: An infinite height need not give an infinite integral
examples.question: Evaluate \(\int_0^4 x^{-\frac12}\,dx\) and decide whether \(\int_0^4 x^{-\frac32}\,dx\) is finite.
examples.solution:
\[\lim_{\varepsilon\to0^+}\left(4-2\sqrt{\varepsilon}\right)=4.\]

The first integral converges. For the second,

\[\left[-2x^{-\frac12}\right]_{\varepsilon}^4=-1+\frac2{\sqrt{\varepsilon}}\longrightarrow+\infty.\]

Thus the second integral diverges; there is no finite value to report. At an infinite upper boundary a separate limit is needed: \(\int_2^\infty x^{-2}\,dx=\lim_{b\to\infty}[-x^{-1}]_2^b=\frac12\).

lessons.title: Recovering a curve from its gradient
lessons.summary: A gradient determines a family. Use a point, tangent or stationary level to select the complete curve.
lessons.objective: Recover a curve with its constant, use geometric information correctly and retain the original gradient domain.
lessons.before: Recall curve points, tangent and normal gradients, stationary points and exact substitution.
lessons.ideas:
A derivative alone leaves a family

If \(f^{\prime}(x)=2x\), every \(f(x)=x^2+C\) has that derivative. A point fixes the vertical constant.

Use the given point after integration

First find an antiderivative with its constant, then substitute both coordinates of the point. Check the final equation against both the derivative and the point.

Position and direction give different equations

A curve point constrains \(f\); a tangent direction constrains \(f^{\prime}\). A finite nonzero normal gradient gives the tangent gradient by a negative reciprocal. A stationary input gives \(f^{\prime}(a)=0\), while a stationary level gives \(f(a)\). Use the correct condition for each unknown.

The original domain remains part of the answer

A recovered expression may have a finite endpoint value even where the supplied gradient was undefined. Unless an extension is specified, keep the original interval. If you rewrite the final curve with \(u=\sqrt{x}\), differentiate and integrate with respect to x first; u is only a convenient answer representation.
lessons.method:
1. Integrate the complete gradient and include its constant.
  2. Use direction or stationary information to determine any gradient parameters.
  3. Substitute the actual curve point or level to find the constant.
  4. Restore every requested coordinate, line and domain; check both original conditions.
mistakes: A slope is not a y-coordinate.
Do not discard the constant when a complete curve is requested.
A normal gradient is not the tangent gradient.
A simplified antiderivative does not change the original domain.

examples.title: A point selects the constant
examples.question: A curve has \(f^{\prime}(x)=6x-4\) and passes through \((2,5)\). Find its equation.
examples.solution:
\[f(x)=3x^2-4x+C.\]

At the point, \(5=12-8+C\), so \(C=1\).

\[y=3x^2-4x+1.\]

This expression gives both the stated gradient and the given point.

examples.title: A fractional-power gradient with an original restriction
examples.question: A curve has \(f^{\prime}(x)=3\sqrt{x}-\frac2{\sqrt{x}}\) for \(x>0\), and \(f(4)=1\). Find f.
examples.solution:
\[f(x)=2x^{\frac32}-4\sqrt{x}+C.\]

At \(x=4\), \(1=16-8+C\), so

\[f(x)=2x^{\frac32}-4\sqrt{x}-7,\quad x>0.\]

The original gradient was supplied only for positive x. In terms of \(u=\sqrt{x}\), the same final curve is \(2u^3-4u-7\).

examples.title: A normal direction and a point fix different constants
examples.question: A curve has \(f^{\prime}(x)=kx-2\). At \((2,3)\) its normal gradient is \(-\frac16\). Find k, the curve and the tangent.
examples.solution:
The tangent gradient is 6, so \(2k-2=6\) and \(k=4\). Integration gives \(f(x)=2x^2-2x+C\). The point gives \(3=8-4+C\), hence \(C=-1\).

\[y=2x^2-2x-1,\qquad y=6x-9\text{ (tangent).}\]

examples.title: A stationary level determines the vertical position
examples.question: A curve has \(f^{\prime}(x)=3x^2-3\) and a local maximum of height 5. Find its equation and both stationary points.
examples.solution:
\[f(x)=x^3-3x+C,\qquad f^{\prime\prime}(x)=6x.\]

The maximum occurs at \(x=-1\); its height is \(2+C=5\), so \(C=3\). The curve is

\[y=x^3-3x+3.\]

Its stationary points are \((-1,5)\), a maximum, and \((1,1)\), a minimum.

lessons.title: Signed integrals and geometric areas
lessons.summary: Sketch or compare the boundaries, find every change of order and add positive pieces of geometric area.
lessons.objective: Distinguish signed accumulation from area, use correct intersections and determine an unknown boundary from an area condition.
lessons.before: Recall roots, intersections, curve signs and definite integration.
lessons.ideas:
An integral can cancel positive and negative pieces

\(\int_a^b f(x)\,dx\) is signed. Geometric area is non-negative. Split at every x-axis crossing where the sign changes, then add the magnitudes of the pieces.

Between two curves use upper minus lower

\[A=\int_a^b\bigl(f(x)-g(x)\bigr)\,dx\quad\text{if }f(x)\ge g(x).\]

Find intersections from the original equations. Check which curve is above on each interval; split again if their order changes. An endpoint can also be a supplied vertical boundary rather than an intersection.

Keep the diagram and limits consistent

A sketch identifies the relevant bounded region; it does not replace the intersection calculation. For a horizontal strip use right minus left with respect to y, and convert the limits to y-values.

An area condition can determine a boundary

Integrate with the unknown endpoint still present. Solve the resulting equation, then filter by the original boundary direction and domain. A second algebraic root may describe the wrong region.
lessons.method:
1. Find the actual boundaries and all relevant intersections.
  2. Determine the signs or upper/lower order on each subinterval.
  3. Integrate the positive difference for each geometric piece.
  4. Add all pieces and restore restrictions on any unknown endpoint.
mistakes: The absolute value of one total integral can still miss area.
Use every change of sign or curve order.
Find intersections before choosing the limits.
A negative boundary root can be inadmissible even when its algebra is correct.

examples.title: Cancellation hides geometric area
examples.question: For \(y=x^2-1\) on \([-2,2]\), find the signed integral and the total area between the curve and the x-axis.
examples.solution:
The roots are \(-1\) and 1. The three signed pieces, in order, are \(\frac43,-\frac43,\frac43\). Thus

\[\int_{-2}^2(x^2-1)\,dx=\frac43,\]\[A=\frac43+\frac43+\frac43=4.\]

Taking the absolute value only after combining the pieces would give the wrong area.

examples.title: Intersections choose the limits
examples.question: Find the area enclosed by \(y=2x\) and \(y=x^2\).
examples.solution:
\[x^2=2x\quad\Rightarrow\quad x=0,2.\]

The line is above the parabola between these inputs, so

\[A=\int_0^2(2x-x^2)\,dx=\left[x^2-\frac{x^3}{3}\right]_0^2=\frac43.\]

examples.title: Two lobes have zero signed sum
examples.question: Find the signed integral and total area for \(y=x^3-x\) between \(x=-1\) and \(x=1\).
examples.solution:
The roots are \(-1,0,1\). The curve is positive on \((-1,0)\) and negative on \((0,1)\). The primitive is \(\frac{x^4}{4}-\frac{x^2}{2}\).

\[I=0,\qquad A=\frac14+\frac14=\frac12.\]

Zero signed change does not mean that no region is enclosed.

examples.title: The required side of the axis selects the root
examples.question: The region under \(y=2x+1\) from \(x=0\) to \(x=b\), where \(b>0\), has area 6. Find b.
examples.solution:
\[b^2+b=6\quad\Rightarrow\quad (b-2)(b+3)=0.\]

The condition \(b>0\) retains only \(b=2\). The root \(-3\) does not describe the specified region to the right of the origin.

lessons.title: Volumes of revolution about either coordinate axis
lessons.summary: Use distance from the axis as the radius and sum circular cross-sections in the matching variable.
lessons.objective: Build disk and washer integrals about either axis, including the hole and the correct transformed boundaries.
lessons.before: Recall area of a circle, curve intersections, rearranging equations and definite integrals.
lessons.ideas:
Cross-sectional area gives volume

Rotating a region touching the x-axis gives disks perpendicular to that axis:

\[V=\pi\int_a^b y^2\,dx.\]

The radius is a distance from the axis. Square the radius, then integrate with respect to the strip direction.

A region away from the axis leaves a hole

\[V=\pi\int_a^b\bigl(R(x)^2-r(x)^2\bigr)\,dx.\]

Use the larger distance for the outer radius and the smaller distance for the inner radius. Subtract the squares; \((R-r)^2\) is the area of a different circle. Check any sign changes relative to the axis before using a washer formula.

About the y-axis use horizontal cross-sections

\[V=\pi\int_c^d\bigl(R(y)^2-r(y)^2\bigr)\,dy.\]

Express x as a function of y and convert the boundaries to y-values. A polynomial in y must be integrated with respect to y. Do not interchange dx and dy while keeping the same integrand and limits.

One region gives different solids about different axes

The axis determines radii and limits. Identify the actual region first; do not rotate the whole area under each curve separately if that would fill an intended hole. Include π and cubic units in the final volume.
lessons.method:
1. Identify the region and the axis of revolution.
  2. Choose cross-sections perpendicular to that axis.
  3. Write outer and inner radii as distances, using the matching variable and limits.
  4. Integrate π times the difference of their squares and check positivity and units.
mistakes: Square radii before subtracting.
Do not omit an inner hole.
About the y-axis convert both the expression and limits.
A final volume needs π and cubic units when lengths have units.

examples.title: A sloping profile gives disks
examples.question: Rotate the region under \(y=1+x\), above the x-axis, from \(x=0\) to 2 about the x-axis. Find its volume.
examples.solution:
\[V=\pi\int_0^2(1+x)^2\,dx=\pi\left[x+x^2+\frac{x^3}{3}\right]_0^2=\frac{26\pi}{3}.\]

The integrand is the square of the entire radius, including its cross term.

examples.title: An inner boundary removes a cone-shaped hole
examples.question: The region \(0\le x\le2\), \(x\le y\le2\) is rotated about the x-axis. Find the volume.
examples.solution:
The outer radius is 2 and the inner radius is x, so

\[V=\pi\int_0^2(4-x^2)\,dx=\frac{16\pi}{3}.\]

Using \((2-x)^2\) would square the thickness instead of subtracting circular areas.

examples.title: A vertical axis changes the integration variable
examples.question: Rotate the region between \(x=0\) and \(x=y^2\), for \(0\le y\le2\), about the y-axis.
examples.solution:
A horizontal strip gives radius \(y^2\). Therefore

\[V=\pi\int_0^2 y^4\,dy=\frac{32\pi}{5}.\]

The limits are y-values, not x-values. The radius must be squared even though x is already a square.

examples.title: The same region, two different axes
examples.question: The curves \(y=x\) and \(y=x^2\) enclose a region in the first quadrant. Find its volumes about the x-axis and about the y-axis.
examples.solution:
The intersections are \((0,0)\) and \((1,1)\). For x-axis rotation,

\[V_x=\pi\int_0^1(x^2-x^4)\,dx=\frac{2\pi}{15}.\]

For y-axis rotation, the outer radius is \(\sqrt{y}\), the inner radius is y:

\[V_y=\pi\int_0^1(y-y^2)\,dy=\frac{\pi}{6}.\]

Both setups use washers, but their radii and integration variables differ.

lessons.title: Constants, parameters and repeated integration
lessons.summary: Separate the constants from successive integrations and combine shape, position and accumulation conditions.
lessons.objective: Recover a curve from a second derivative, determine parameters, recognise a useful derivative and interpret net accumulation.
lessons.before: Recall first and second derivatives, initial conditions, signed integrals and stationary-point classification.
lessons.ideas:
Two integrations produce two independent constants

\[f^{\prime\prime}(x)\ \longrightarrow\ f^{\prime}(x)+\text{first constant}\ \longrightarrow\ f(x)+\text{second constant}.\]

Use a gradient condition for the first derivative and a point condition for the function. A stationary condition supplies a zero gradient. Do not reuse one constant as if both conditions described the same quantity.

A coefficient and an integration constant are different unknowns

Use the supplied gradient, point, area or stationary information in the appropriate original expression. Solve the complete system and check it before drawing conclusions about the curve.

A known derivative can identify an integral

Differentiate a proposed product using expansion or the chain rule. If its derivative is a constant multiple of the required integrand, reverse that relation. This is a recognition method, not a requirement to introduce integration by parts or a new nonlinear substitution technique.

Integrating a rate gives signed change

\[A(t)=A(0)+\int_0^t q(v)\,dv.\]

When the rate changes sign, the accumulated amount may start falling even though earlier accumulation was positive. A maximum amount is found from the sign of the rate and comparison with the interval endpoints.
lessons.method:
1. Identify which expression each condition constrains.
  2. Keep a separate constant for each integration.
  3. Solve and restore the original derivative and value conditions.
  4. For a mixed problem check signs, boundaries, units and the meaning of the requested quantity.
mistakes: A condition on f′ does not directly determine f.
Two integrations need two independently determined constants.
A negative later rate reduces an earlier accumulated amount.
Recognising a derivative still requires checking its full multiplier.

examples.title: A gradient condition and a point condition
examples.question: Given \(f^{\prime\prime}(x)=12x-6\), \(f^{\prime}(1)=3\) and \(f(0)=2\), find f.
examples.solution:
\[f^{\prime}(x)=6x^2-6x+C_1.\]

The gradient condition gives \(C_1=3\). Integrate again:

\[f(x)=2x^3-3x^2+3x+C_2.\]

The point gives \(C_2=2\). Each constant belongs to a different integration.

examples.title: Recover a gradient coefficient before the vertical constant
examples.question: A curve has \(f^{\prime}(x)=ax^2-2\), \(f^{\prime}(1)=4\) and \(f(1)=1\). Find a and f.
examples.solution:
The first condition gives \(a-2=4\), so \(a=6\). Then

\[f(x)=2x^3-2x+C.\]

The point gives \(1=2-2+C\), hence \(f(x)=2x^3-2x+1\).

examples.title: A final amount can be below its earlier maximum
examples.question: A model has \(A(0)=10\) and \(A^{\prime}(t)=4-t\) for \(0\le t\le6\). Find A, the final amount and the greatest amount.
examples.solution:
\[A(t)=10+4t-\frac{t^2}{2}.\]

The rate changes from positive to negative at \(t=4\), so the greatest amount is \(A(4)=18\). The final amount is \(A(6)=16\). The last interval removes 2 from the previously reached maximum.

examples.title: Use a derivative to evaluate a less obvious integral
examples.question: Differentiate \(F(x)=x^2(x+1)^3\). Hence evaluate \(\int_0^1 x(x+1)^2(5x+2)\,dx\).
examples.solution:
Expanding before differentiating, or differentiating the product, gives

\[F^{\prime}(x)=x(x+1)^2(5x+2).\]

The required integrand is precisely this derivative, so

\[I=F(1)-F(0)=8.\]

There is no need to invent a separate integration rule for the product.

questions.title: A complete antiderivative with a specified constant
questions.prompt_html: Find \(F(x)\) such that \(F^{\prime}(x)=6 x^{2} - 4 x + 3\) and \(F(0)=0\). Then select why the unrestricted indefinite integral also needs a constant.
questions.answer_html:
Complete function F(x): \(2 x^{3} - 2 x^{2} + 3 x\)

Why include C without the condition?: Every constant has zero derivative
questions.solution_html:
Integrate every term, then use \(F(0)=0\). Without that value condition, adding a constant leaves the derivative unchanged.

Complete answers

Complete function F(x): \(2 x^{3} - 2 x^{2} + 3 x\)

Why include C without the condition?: Every constant has zero derivative
questions.hint_html: Rewrite powers, reverse the derivative and retain the limits or supplied normalising condition.

fields.label: Why include C without the condition?

options.A: A derivative determines one vertical position
options.C: A constant is needed only for negative powers

marking_criteria.description_html: Complete correct answer for Complete function F(x).
Complete correct answer for Why include C without the condition?.

questions.title: A whole linear-power primitive
questions.prompt_html: Given \(F^{\prime}(x)=\left(2 x + 1\right)^{3}\) and \(F(- \frac{1}{2})=0\), give the complete F. Also evaluate \(\int_{0}^{1}\left(2 x + 1\right)^{3}\,dx\).
questions.answer_html:
Complete function F(x): \(2 x^{4} + 4 x^{3} + 3 x^{2} + x + \frac{1}{8}\)

Definite integral: \(10\)
questions.solution_html:
Divide by both the new power and the inner gradient. The normalising input makes the inner expression zero. For the definite integral use upper minus lower.

Complete answers

Complete function F(x): \(2 x^{4} + 4 x^{3} + 3 x^{2} + x + \frac{1}{8}\)

Definite integral: \(10\)
questions.hint_html: Rewrite powers, reverse the derivative and retain the limits or supplied normalising condition.

marking_criteria.description_html: Complete correct answer for Complete function F(x).
Complete correct answer for Definite integral.

questions.title: A signed integral and its reversal
questions.answer_html:
Integral with increasing limits: \(- \frac{4}{3}\)

Integral with reversed limits: \(\frac{4}{3}\)
questions.solution_html:
The integrand is non-positive on the interval. Reversing the limits negates the signed result; it does not change the integrand.

Complete answers

Integral with increasing limits: \(- \frac{4}{3}\)

Integral with reversed limits: \(\frac{4}{3}\)
questions.hint_html: Rewrite powers, reverse the derivative and retain the limits or supplied normalising condition.

marking_criteria.description_html: Complete correct answer for Integral with increasing limits.
Complete correct answer for Integral with reversed limits.

questions.title: An improper endpoint with a finite limit
questions.prompt_html: Evaluate \(\int_{0}^{4}\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}\,dx\) using a limit. Use the power-rule primitive with no added constant. Give its limit at the improper boundary and decide whether the integral converges.
questions.answer_html:
Limit of the selected primitive at the improper boundary: \(0\)

Value of the improper integral: \(4\)

Conclusion: Converges to a finite value
questions.solution_html:
Evaluate the primitive on a finite interior interval first. At the improper boundary take the appropriate limit. A finite primitive difference gives the convergent value even when an endpoint is undefined or infinite.

Complete answers

Limit of the selected primitive at the improper boundary: \(0\)

Value of the improper integral: \(4\)

Conclusion: Converges to a finite value
questions.hint_html: Rewrite powers, reverse the derivative and retain the limits or supplied normalising condition.

fields.label: Limit of the selected primitive at the improper boundary

options.B: Diverges because the integrand is undefined at zero
options.C: It is an ordinary integral of a continuous function at zero

marking_criteria.description_html: Complete correct answer for Limit of the selected primitive at the improper boundary.
Complete correct answer for Value of the improper integral.

questions.title: A gradient and a point give the whole curve
questions.prompt_html: A curve has \(f^{\prime}(x)=6 x - 4\) and passes through \(\left( 2, \ 5\right)\). Give the integration constant C in \(f(x)=3 x^{2} - 4 x+C\) and the complete f.
questions.answer_html:
Integration constant C: \(1\)

Complete function f(x): \(3 x^{2} - 4 x + 1\)
questions.solution_html:
Integrate the entire gradient, substitute both point coordinates, and restore the constant in the final expression.

Complete answers

Integration constant C: \(1\)

Complete function f(x): \(3 x^{2} - 4 x + 1\)
questions.hint_html: Integrate first; then use each original direction, point and domain condition in the appropriate expression.

marking_criteria.description_html: Complete correct answer for Integration constant C.
Complete correct answer for Complete function f(x).

questions.title: A complete fractional-power curve and its domain
questions.prompt_html: For \(x>0\), \(f^{\prime}(x)=3 \sqrt{x} - \frac{2}{\sqrt{x}}\) and \(f(4)=1\). Integrate with respect to x, then use \(u=\sqrt{x}\) to write the complete f as a polynomial in u. Give C and retain the stated x-domain.
questions.answer_html:
Complete f in u = sqrt(x): \(2 u^{3} - 4 u - 7\)

Integration constant C: \(-7\)

Original x-domain: \((0,\infty)\)
questions.solution_html:
Integrate the positive and negative half-powers in x. Use the given point for C, then rewrite the final expression in u. An endpoint extension was not specified.

Complete answers

Complete f in u = sqrt(x): \(2 u^{3} - 4 u - 7\)

Integration constant C: \(-7\)

Original x-domain: \((0,\infty)\)
questions.hint_html: Integrate first; then use each original direction, point and domain condition in the appropriate expression.

marking_criteria.description_html: Complete correct answer for Complete f in u = sqrt(x).

questions.title: A normal direction and a point fix different unknowns
questions.prompt_html: A curve has \(f^{\prime}(x)=kx-2\). At \(\left( 2, \ 3\right)\) its normal gradient is \(- \frac{1}{6}\). Find k, the complete curve and the tangent equation.
questions.answer_html:
Gradient parameter k: \(4\)

Complete f(x): \(2 x^{2} - 2 x - 1\)

Complete tangent equation: \(- 6 x + y + 9\)
questions.solution_html:
Take the negative reciprocal for the tangent gradient. Use it in the gradient condition to find k, then integrate and use the point for C. The tangent goes through that same point.

Complete answers

Gradient parameter k: \(4\)

Complete f(x): \(2 x^{2} - 2 x - 1\)

Complete tangent equation: \(- 6 x + y + 9\)

questions.title: A stationary height selects a curve
questions.prompt_html: A curve has \(f^{\prime}(x)=3 x^{2} - 3\) and its local maximum has height 5. Give the complete f and all stationary points.
questions.solution_html:
Classify the two derivative roots before using the maximum level to fix C. Restore both stationary ordinates using the completed curve.

Complete answers

Complete f(x): \(x^{3} - 3 x + 3\)

All stationary points (x,y): \(\{(-1,\ 5),\ (1,\ 1)\}\)

questions.title: Signed pieces and total geometric area
questions.prompt_html: For \(y=x^{2} - 1\) on \([-2,2]\), give every zero, the signed integral and the total area between the graph and the x-axis.
questions.answer_html:
All zeros in the interval: \(\{-1,\ 1\}\)

Signed integral: \(\frac{4}{3}\)

Total geometric area: \(4\)
questions.solution_html:
Split at both roots. Add the signed pieces for the integral and their positive magnitudes for area. One absolute value after adding all pieces misses cancellation.

Complete answers

All zeros in the interval: \(\{-1,\ 1\}\)

Signed integral: \(\frac{4}{3}\)

Total geometric area: \(4\)

questions.title: Intersections and the upper boundary
questions.prompt_html: Find all intersection points of \(y=2x\) and \(y=x^2\), and the area enclosed by them.
questions.solution_html:
Solve the original intersection equation. The line is above the parabola between the two roots, so integrate line minus curve over that interval.

Complete answers

All intersection points (x,y): \(\{(0,\ 0),\ (2,\ 4)\}\)

Enclosed area: \(\frac{4}{3}\)

questions.title: Two lobes require two positive pieces
questions.prompt_html: For \(y=x^{3} - x\) between \(x=-1\) and \(x=1\), give all zero locations, the signed integral and the sum of the two enclosed areas.
questions.answer_html:
All zero locations: \(\{-1,\ 0,\ 1\}\)

Signed integral: \(0\)

Total area of both lobes: \(\frac{1}{2}\)
questions.solution_html:
The integrand is odd, so its signed integral over symmetric limits is zero. Each lobe has nonzero area; split at zero and add their magnitudes.

Complete answers

All zero locations: \(\{-1,\ 0,\ 1\}\)

questions.prompt_html:
A curve has \(\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}=6 x\). It has a stationary point P\(\left(2,5\right)\).

  1. Determine the nature of the stationary point P.

    [2]

  2. Find the equation of the curve.

    [7]

  3. Find the other stationary point and determine its nature.

    [3]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

At P the second derivative is \(12\). Its sign gives a minimum.

(b)

Increase each power by one, then divide by the new power and any constant inner multiplier. Include a constant for an indefinite integral.

\[\begin{aligned}&\int\left(6 x\right)\,dx\\ &=3 x^{2}+C\end{aligned}\]

Use stationarity at \(2\) to fix the first integration constant: \(C_1=-12\). Thus

\[\frac{dy}{dx}=3 x^{2} - 12\]

Increase each power by one, then divide by the new power and any constant inner multiplier. Include a constant for an indefinite integral.

\[\begin{aligned}&\int\left(3 x^{2} - 12\right)\,dx\\ &=x^{3} - 12 x+C\end{aligned}\]

Use the given point in the integrated expression:

\[C=5-(-16)=21\]\[y=x^{3} - 12 x + 21\]

(c)

Use \(\frac{d}{dx}x^n=nx^{n-1}\), with the chain multiplier for a composite power.

\[\frac{dy}{dx}=3 x^{2} - 12\]\[\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}=6 x\]

Set the first derivative equal to zero and keep every solution in the stated domain.

\[3 \left(x - 2\right) \left(x + 2\right) = 0\]

At \(x=2\), \(\left(2,5\right)\) lies on the curve and \(\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}=12\). It is a minimum.

At \(x=1\), the second derivative is \(-16\) < 0, so P is a maximum.

questions.title: An integral with an improper endpoint
questions.prompt_html:
Evaluate \(\int_{2}^{\infty}\left(\frac{3}{x^{2}}\right)\,dx\).

  1. Evaluate the integral exactly, showing the endpoint limit used.

    [3]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Increase each power by one, then divide by the new power and any constant inner multiplier. Include a constant for an indefinite integral.

\[\begin{aligned}&\int\left(\frac{3}{x^{2}}\right)\,dx\\ &=- \frac{3}{x}+C\end{aligned}\]

Replace the infinite upper limit by b and take the limit as b increases without bound. The primitive has the finite limiting value \(0\).

\[\begin{aligned}&\int_{2}^{\infty}\left(\frac{3}{x^{2}}\right)\,dx\\ &=\left[- \frac{3}{x}\right]_{2}^{\infty}\\ &=\frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}\]

questions.title: A curve and the chord between two of its points
questions.prompt_html:

    [6]

(a)

Use \(\frac{d}{dx}x^n=nx^{n-1}\), with the chain multiplier for a composite power.

\[\frac{dy}{dx}=4 - \frac{32}{\left(2 x - 1\right)^{3}}\]\[\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}=\frac{192}{\left(2 x - 1\right)^{4}}\]

Set the first derivative equal to zero and keep every solution in the stated domain.

(b)

The chord joins the two stated boundary points. Its equation is

questions.prompt_html:
The curve is \(y=- x^{3} + 4 x^{2}\). P has x-coordinate \(3\). The shaded region is bounded by the curve arc from P to its positive x-intercept B, the x-axis from B to the tangent intercept T, and tangent PT.

    [2]

(a)

Use \(\frac{d}{dx}x^n=nx^{n-1}\), with the chain multiplier for a composite power.

\[\frac{dy}{dx}=x \left(8 - 3 x\right)\]

At \(x=3\), the curve point is \(\left(3,9\right)\) and the tangent gradient is \(-3\).

\[y - 9 = 9 - 3 x\]\[y=18 - 3 x\]

(b)

The positive curve intercept is \(4\), and the tangent meets the x-axis at \(6\). Split the region where the lower boundary changes:

Write the tangent and curve ordinates at x as \(y_T\) and \(y_C\), respectively.

\[A=\int_{3}^{4}(y_T-y_C)\,dx+\int_{4}^{6}y_T\,dx\]

Increase each power by one, then divide by the new power and any constant inner multiplier. Include a constant for an indefinite integral.

\[\begin{aligned}&\int\left(- x^{2} \left(4 - x\right) - 3 x + 18\right)\,dx\\ &=\begin{aligned}&\frac{x^{4}}{4}- \frac{4 x^{3}}{3}\\ &- \frac{3 x^{2}}{2}+18 x\end{aligned}+C\end{aligned}\]\[\begin{aligned}&\int_{3}^{4}\left(- x^{2} \left(4 - x\right) - 3 x + 18\right)\,dx\\ &=\left[\begin{aligned}&\frac{x^{4}}{4}- \frac{4 x^{3}}{3}\\ &- \frac{3 x^{2}}{2}+18 x\end{aligned}\right]_{3}^{4}\\ &=\frac{23}{12}\end{aligned}\]

Increase each power by one, then divide by the new power and any constant inner multiplier. Include a constant for an indefinite integral.

\[\begin{aligned}&\int\left(18 - 3 x\right)\,dx\\ &=- \frac{3 x^{2}}{2} + 18 x+C\end{aligned}\]\[\begin{aligned}&\int_{4}^{6}\left(18 - 3 x\right)\,dx\\ &=\left[- \frac{3 x^{2}}{2} + 18 x\right]_{4}^{6}\\ &=6\end{aligned}\]

(c)

Only abscissae are multiplied by \(\frac{2}{3}\). The same factor multiplies every horizontal width, so the area is multiplied by \(\frac{2}{3}\).

(a)

Take radii perpendicular to the x-axis. Subtract the squared inner radius from the squared outer radius; do not square their difference.

Here the outer radius is \(R=\frac{9}{\left(2 x - 1\right)^{2}}\) and the inner radius is \(r=1\).

(b)

Use \(\frac{d}{dx}x^n=nx^{n-1}\), with the chain multiplier for a composite power.

\[\frac{dy}{dx}=- \frac{36}{\left(2 x - 1\right)^{3}}\]

At \(x=2\), the curve point is \(\left(2,1\right)\) and the tangent gradient is \(- \frac{4}{3}\).

\[y - 1 = \frac{8}{3} - \frac{4 x}{3}\]\[y=\frac{11}{3} - \frac{4 x}{3}\]

\[y=\frac{11}{3} - \frac{4 x}{3}\]\[y=\frac{3 x}{4} - \frac{1}{2}\]

Their axis intercepts are \(\frac{11}{4}\) and \(\frac{2}{3}\). The vertical height of the triangle is 1, so its area is \(\frac12\left|\frac{11}{4}-(\frac{2}{3})\right|=\frac{25}{24}\).

questions.prompt_html:
The curve is \(y=\frac{25}{\left(4 x - 3\right)^{2}}\), for \(x>\frac{3}{4}\). The shaded region is between the curve, y = 1 and \(x=1\), on the branch shown.

  1. Find the exact volume when the shaded region makes one complete revolution about the x-axis.

    [5]

  2. At B, where the curve meets y = 1, its tangent and normal meet the x-axis at T and N. Find the exact area of triangle BTN.

    [5]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Take radii perpendicular to the x-axis. Subtract the squared inner radius from the squared outer radius; do not square their difference.

Here the outer radius is \(R=\frac{25}{\left(4 x - 3\right)^{2}}\) and the inner radius is \(r=1\).

\[V=\pi\int_{1}^{2}(R^2-r^2)\,dx\]

Increase each power by one, then divide by the new power and any constant inner multiplier. Include a constant for an indefinite integral.

\[\begin{aligned}&\int\left(-1 + \frac{625}{\left(4 x - 3\right)^{4}}\right)\,dx\\ &=- x - \frac{625}{12 \left(4 x - 3\right)^{3}}+C\end{aligned}\]\[\begin{aligned}&\int_{1}^{2}\left(-1 + \frac{625}{\left(4 x - 3\right)^{4}}\right)\,dx\\ &=\left[- x - \frac{625}{12 \left(4 x - 3\right)^{3}}\right]_{1}^{2}\\ &=\frac{152}{3}\end{aligned}\]\[V=\frac{152 \pi}{3}\]

(b)

Use \(\frac{d}{dx}x^n=nx^{n-1}\), with the chain multiplier for a composite power.

\[\frac{dy}{dx}=- \frac{200}{\left(4 x - 3\right)^{3}}\]

At \(x=2\), the curve point is \(\left(2,1\right)\) and the tangent gradient is \(- \frac{8}{5}\).

\[y - 1 = \frac{16}{5} - \frac{8 x}{5}\]\[y=\frac{21}{5} - \frac{8 x}{5}\]

The normal has gradient \(\frac{5}{8}\). The two line equations are

\[y=\frac{21}{5} - \frac{8 x}{5}\]\[y=\frac{5 x}{8} - \frac{1}{4}\]

Their axis intercepts are \(\frac{21}{8}\) and \(\frac{2}{5}\). The vertical height of the triangle is 1, so its area is \(\frac12\left|\frac{21}{8}-(\frac{2}{5})\right|=\frac{89}{80}\).

questions.title: A chord and a sideways parabola
questions.prompt_html:
The curve \(x=y^2+5\) contains A\(\left(21,-4\right)\) and B\(\left(30,5\right)\). The shaded region lies between chord AB and the curve.

  2. Find the exact volume when the shaded region makes one complete revolution about the y-axis.

    [5]

The two points have y-coordinates \(-4\) and \(5\). Their x-coordinates are \(21\) and \(30\). The line expressed in the required variables is \(x=y + 25\).

Take radii perpendicular to the y-axis. Subtract the squared inner radius from the squared outer radius; do not square their difference.

Here the outer radius is \(R=y + 25\) and the inner radius is \(r=y^{2} + 5\).

\[V=\pi\int_{-4}^{5}(R^2-r^2)\,dy\]

\[\begin{aligned}&\int\left(- y^{4} - 9 y^{2} + 50 y + 600\right)\,dy\\ &=- \frac{y^{5}}{5} - 3 y^{3} + 25 y^{2} + 600 y+C\end{aligned}\]\[\begin{aligned}&\int_{-4}^{5}\left(- y^{4} - 9 y^{2} + 50 y + 600\right)\,dy\\ &=\left[- \frac{y^{5}}{5} - 3 y^{3} + 25 y^{2} + 600 y\right]_{-4}^{5}\\ &=\frac{21141}{5}\end{aligned}\]\[V=\frac{21141 \pi}{5}\]

questions.title: Revolution of a region between two positive boundaries
questions.prompt_html:
On \(x>-1\), the shaded region is enclosed by \(y=\frac{3}{x + 1}\) and \(y=\frac{15}{8} - \frac{3 x}{8}\).

  1. Find both intersection points.

    [3]

  2. Find the exact volume when the shaded region makes one complete revolution about the x-axis.

    [5]

  3. Find the point on this curve branch where the tangent is parallel to the straight boundary.

    [3]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Equate the curve and line, with x > \(-1\). Clearing the positive denominator gives a quadratic whose roots are \(1\) and \(3\). Substitute in either boundary for their matching ordinates.

(b)

Take radii perpendicular to the x-axis. Subtract the squared inner radius from the squared outer radius; do not square their difference.

Here the outer radius is \(R=\frac{15}{8} - \frac{3 x}{8}\) and the inner radius is \(r=\frac{3}{x + 1}\).

\[V=\pi\int_{1}^{3}(R^2-r^2)\,dx\]

Increase each power by one, then divide by the new power and any constant inner multiplier. Include a constant for an indefinite integral.

\[\begin{aligned}&\int\left(\begin{aligned}&\frac{9 x^{2}}{64}- \frac{45 x}{32}\\ &+\frac{225}{64}\\ &- \frac{9}{\left(x + 1\right)^{2}}\end{aligned}\right)\,dx\\ &=\begin{aligned}&\frac{3 x^{3}}{64}- \frac{45 x^{2}}{64}\\ &+\frac{225 x}{64}+\frac{9}{x + 1}\end{aligned}+C\end{aligned}\]\[\begin{aligned}&\int_{1}^{3}\left(\begin{aligned}&\frac{9 x^{2}}{64}- \frac{45 x}{32}\\ &+\frac{225}{64}\\ &- \frac{9}{\left(x + 1\right)^{2}}\end{aligned}\right)\,dx\\ &=\left[\begin{aligned}&\frac{3 x^{3}}{64}- \frac{45 x^{2}}{64}\\ &+\frac{225 x}{64}+\frac{9}{x + 1}\end{aligned}\right]_{1}^{3}\\ &=\frac{3}{8}\end{aligned}\]\[V=\frac{3 \pi}{8}\]

(c)

The straight boundary gradient is \(- \frac{3}{8}\). Set the curve derivative equal to it:

\[- \frac{3}{\left(x + 1\right)^{2}} = - \frac{3}{8}\]

This gives \((x+1)^2=8\). The branch condition \(x>-1\) selects the positive square root, giving the stated point.
